                                     PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                      §
 TRANSMISSION COST                             §                  OF TEXAS
 RECOVERY IN THE ERCOT                         §
 REGION                                        §


                                COMMENTS OF HUT 8 CORP

I.     INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF INTEREST
Hut 8 Corp (“Hut 8”) appreciates the opportunity to file these comments in response to the Proposal
for Publication (“PFP”) of new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §25.252 and amendments
to §25.192 and §25.193, as approved by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”)
at its July 9, 2026 open meeting in Project No. 58000. Hut 8 is a large load customer operating
computationally intensive operations such as Bitcoin mining and high-performance computing
facilities within the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) power region and therefore
has a direct and substantial interest in the Commission’s rules governing large load interconnection
standards, transmission and distribution cost recovery, and tariff terms applicable to large load
customers.

Hut 8 submits these comments both to raise a threshold concern regarding the relationship between
this proceeding and Project No. 58481 and to respond to the specific questions posed by
Commission Staff in the PFP.

II.    ALIGN PROJECT NOS. 58000 AND 58481 BEFORE MOVING FORWARD

Project Nos. 58000 and 58481 are tackling the same problem from two different angles: making
sure large load customers — not other transmission ratepayers in ERCOT— cover the cost of the
transmission and distribution build-out required to serve their large loads. Project No. 58481
handles this on the interconnection side, through upfront payments and security deposits before a
project connects. Project No. 58000 handles it on the ratemaking side, through minimum demand
charges and how utilities recover those costs. Because Commission is seeking to solve the same
problem with different tools from different perspectives in two different dockets, we are concerned
that large load customers could end up paying for the same infrastructure twice — once upfront
through payments and security under §25.194, and again if those same costs get folded into utility
rates under §25.252(k) without credit for what those customers will pay as part of their obligations
under § 25.194. Hut 8 recognizes that the Commission is still finalizing the language for 58481
and provides these comments for consideration ahead of its ultimate adoption.




                                                   1
 Therefore, Hut 8 respectfully requests the Commission:

(1) Coordinate the two dockets, or at least ensure adequate coordination them so that the final rules
adopted in each are property aligned and do not result in double-charging large load customers for
the same costs; and
(2) Add language to §25.192(k) confirming that any security or fees credited against a utility's
rates account for amounts a customer has already paid or secured for the same costs under §25.194.

(3) No duplicate recovery or credit. Amounts applied as an offset to a TSP’s transmission revenue
requirement under this subsection must not duplicate any amount paid, secured, reimbursed,
forfeited, or otherwise credited by a large load customer for the same costs under §25.194 of this
title. A TSP must identify and exclude from any offset under this subsection any interconnection
fee, financial security, contribution in aid of construction, or other customer-funded amount that
corresponds to costs already paid or secured under §25.194.

III.   RESPONSE TO THE COMMISSION’S QUESTIONS
Below are Hut 8’s answers to the six questions Commission Staff asked about in the PFP.

1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different non-
coincident (NCP) demands?
Hut 8 believes minimum billing demand values should be set based on how flexible and curtailable
a load is — not just its size. A single demand charge applied to every large load customer, no
matter their contracted peak demand, NCP demand, or ability to curtail quickly, doesn’t reflect
how differently these customers actually contribute to stranded-cost and reliability risk. That said,
flexibility should be locked in contractually — for example, through a Controllable Load Resource
program — rather than assumed from how a customer currently operates today, so ERCOT can
actually count on that flexibility.

2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be (a) fixed for 20 years as proposed, (b)
reduced in phases over a period of 20 years, or (c) extended to a longer time period?
Hut 8 supports option (b) — a phased reduction over the 20-year period. That approach more
closely tracks the actual risk that the charge is intended to address: as a load runs at its contracted
peak capacity, the customer’s own billing payments are paying back the cost of bringing that load
online, diminishing the stranded-cost risk that justifies a high minimum billing demand and
reducing the need for such a charge. A flat floor held constant for two decades doesn’t reflect this
reality, instead it continues to cover for a risk long after it is an actual concern.

To preserve cost causation, the Commission should consider that minimum billing demand be
calibrated to the unrecovered transmission costs reasonably attributable to serving the large load
customer, net of amounts already recovered through the customer’s transmission charges,


                                                  2
 interconnection payments, contributions in aid of construction, forfeited financial security, or other
customer-funded amounts. As the customer operates at or near its contracted peak capacity, those
ongoing payments reduce the risk that transmission facilities built or reserved for the customer
will become stranded or underutilized. The minimum billing demand should therefore decline over
time in a transparent manner that reflects the decreasing unrecovered cost exposure.

3. Should the large load minimum billing demand instead reflect a “ratcheted” demand or a
“weighted average” minimum billing demand, and should any such percentage decline in
phases over the years?
Between the two, Hut 8 favors a ratcheted structure — the minimum billing demand set as a
declining percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand, phased
down over time. A ratchet ties what a customer pays more closely to its actual use than a weighted-
average approach would, while still giving TSPs and DSPs cost-recovery certainty in the early,
riskiest years after interconnection.

4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load (an entity subject to
§25.194 in which 50% or greater of site demand consists of power-electronic-based
computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities)?
No. A megawatt pulled from the grid costs the same to serve whether it's powering a data center,
a factory, or anything else — the use case doesn't change the cost math. Size and risk are already
handled through contracted peak demand and NCP demand, the same metrics behind the minimum
billing demand mechanism (see our answer to Question 1). And computational loads aren't all alike
— flexibility and curtailability vary considerably from one facility to the next, so lumping them
all into one rate bucket risks overcharging some and undercharging others. If any differentiation
makes sense, it should track actual flexibility and curtailability — through something like a
Controllable Load Resource program — not whether the load happens to be computational.

5. Should the definition of transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission
capacity needs of a particular load?
Hut 8 recommends no change be made to the definition of transmission interconnection costs.
Batch-study upgrades usually benefit more than just the customer whose request triggered the
study; they help the wider transmission system too. One customer should not be responsible for
the full cost if many other customers will actually benefit from the outcome. Putting the entire
cost on the customer whose request triggered the study risks shifting system-wide benefits onto
individual large load customers. If the definition does get expanded, it should only cover costs
clearly and solely tied to that specific customer’s own interconnection request and that do not
benefit other customers.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether it has
energized or is fully using available capacity, how should these loads be reflected in resource
adequacy reports, assessments, and transmission planning studies?


                                                  3
 Hut 8 recommends that ERCOT’s resource adequacy and transmission planning studies use the
realistic, milestone-based energization schedules customers are required to disclose under
§25.194, instead of reflecting a customer’s full contracted peak demand as in-use from day one.
That keeps planning studies from overbuilding or overcounting speculative load, while still
accounting for real future need through the disclosure and milestone process already in place —
and it better reflects how computational loads actually ramp up and can flex over time.

IV.    CONCLUSION
In short, Hut 8 asks the Commission to (1) coordinate or consolidate Project Nos. 58000 and 58481
and sequence their adoption to avoid conflicting or duplicative requirements — especially around
financial security and cost recovery for transmission and system-upgrade costs; and (2) consider
our responses below in future drafts of both Project Nos. 58000 and 58481.

                                                  Respectfully submitted,

                                                  Casey Bell
                                                  State Bar No. 24012271
                                                  BALCH & BINGHAM LLP
                                                  600 Congress Avenue, Suite 2700
                                                  Austin, Texas 78701
                                                  Telephone: (512) 744-9300
                                                  Facsimile: (512) 744-9399
                                                  Email: cabell@balch.com

                                            By:      /s/ Casey Bell
                                                     Casey Bell

                                                  ATTORNEY FOR HUT 8 CORP.




                                               4
                                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
                                   Submitted by: Hut 8 Corp

Hut 8 Corp’s comments in Project No. 58000 make the following substantive recommendations:

• Coordinate or consolidate this project with Project No. 58481 — the PFP here is built directly
on terms and mechanics from §25.194, which is still pending in Project No. 58481.

• Finalize §25.194 before or concurrently with this project, to ensure cross-references in §25.252
match the final §25.194 text.

• Add language to §25.252(k) so large load customers aren’t required to pay the same transmission
and system-upgrade costs twice — once through security under §25.194, and again through the
rate offset in §25.252(k).

• Differentiate minimum billing demand values based on load flexibility and curtailability,

• Adopt a phased reduction (rather than a 20-year fixed floor) for the minimum billing demand.

• If a phase-down mechanism is adopted, use a ratcheted structure rather than a weighted-average
structure.

• Do not create separate rate treatment for large computational loads (data centers and crypto
mining) based on end use — the grid doesn’t care what the power is used for, and size/risk is
already covered by contracted peak demand and NCP demand.

• Don’t broaden “transmission interconnection costs” to include batch-study-recommended
projects — any broadening should be strictly limited to costs tied to a specific customer’s request.

• Base resource adequacy and transmission planning treatment of reserved capacity on realistic,
milestone-based energization schedules rather than full contracted peak demand from the date of
reservation.
